notes:
1. Five-Year Plan Assessment — Meaning and Scope

  • Assessment of Five-Year Plans examines how far planned development achieved India's economic and social objectives.
  • A Plan must be judged through both economic performance and broader development outcomes.
  • Important areas include national-income growth, agriculture, industry, employment, poverty reduction, infrastructure, human development, regional balance, self-reliance and social justice.
📌 Must-Memorise

Plan Assessment → Growth + Development Outcomes

2. Plan Success — Growth Rate Is Not Enough

  • Achievement of the targeted growth rate alone does not prove that a Plan was successful.
  • Employment creation, poverty reduction, food security, infrastructure, human development and distribution of benefits must also be examined.
  • Each Plan must also be judged in the historical context in which it operated.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Plan Success ≠ Growth Rate Alone

3. Evolution of Planning Priorities

Indian planning broadly moved through:

Agricultural Recovery

→ Industrialisation

→ Self-Reliance

→ Poverty Reduction

→ Modernisation

→ Human Development

→ Inclusive Growth

→ Sustainable Development

📌 Must-Memorise

Planning Priorities Changed with India's Development Needs

4. First Five-Year Plan — 1951–1956

  • India entered the First Plan facing food shortages, refugee rehabilitation, inflation, weak infrastructure and low agricultural productivity.
  • Agriculture received high priority along with irrigation, power and rural development.
  • Agricultural production improved during the Plan period.
  • Investment in irrigation and multipurpose river-valley projects strengthened India's productive base.
  • Major projects included Bhakra-Nangal, Hirakud and Damodar Valley.
  • Community Development Programme and National Extension Service expanded organised rural-development activity.
  • Economic growth exceeded the original target.
  • The Plan also helped restore economic stability after the disruptions of Independence and Partition.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Plan → Agriculture + Irrigation + Stability

5. First Plan — Limitations and Overall Assessment

  • Agricultural productivity remained low despite improvement in output.
  • Rural poverty continued to be widespread.
  • Industrial capacity remained limited.
  • India remained predominantly poor and agrarian.
  • The First Plan is nevertheless generally regarded as one of the more successful early Five-Year Plans because it created a stable agricultural and infrastructural foundation.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Plan → Successful Foundation, Not Complete Transformation

6. Second Five-Year Plan — 1956–1961

  • The Second Plan was strongly influenced by the Mahalanobis strategy.
  • Heavy industries and capital-goods production received major priority.
  • Public-sector investment expanded substantially.
  • The State took a leading role in basic and heavy industries.
  • Major steel plants developed during this period included Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur.
  • Engineering industries, machine-building capacity, power projects and basic industries expanded.
  • India developed a stronger domestic ability to manufacture industrial equipment.
  • Technical and scientific institutions also expanded.
📌 Must-Memorise

Second Plan → Heavy-Industrial Foundation

7. Second Plan — Major Weaknesses

  • Agriculture received lower relative priority than heavy industry.
  • Food shortages remained a major concern.
  • Limited agricultural and consumer-goods supply contributed to price pressures.
  • Heavy industry was capital-intensive and therefore did not generate employment on the scale required by India's growing labour force.
  • Large public-sector investment placed pressure on government finances.
  • Imports of machinery, technology and intermediate goods increased pressure on foreign exchange.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Industrial Success ≠ Balanced Sectoral Development

8. Second Plan — Overall Assessment

  • The Second Plan created the basic heavy-industrial foundation of modern India.
  • Its long-term industrial contribution was substantial.
  • Agriculture, employment, consumer-goods availability and foreign-exchange pressure remained major weaknesses.
📌 Must-Memorise

Second Plan → Strong Industrial Base + Weak Agriculture and Employment

9. Third Five-Year Plan — 1961–1966

  • The Third Plan aimed to establish a self-reliant and self-generating economy.
  • It attempted to balance agricultural development with continued industrialisation.
  • Its performance was severely disrupted by the India-China War of 1962 and the India-Pakistan War of 1965.
  • Defence and emergency expenditure diverted resources away from planned development.
  • Severe droughts reduced agricultural production.
  • Food shortages intensified and dependence on imported food increased.
  • Resource constraints and agricultural failure weakened economic growth.
  • The Plan failed to achieve many of its major development targets.
📌 Must-Memorise

Third Plan Shocks → Wars + Drought + Food Crisis

10. Third Plan — Overall Assessment and Major Lesson

  • The Third Plan substantially underperformed.
  • Its experience demonstrated that industrial development could not be sustained without adequate food production and agricultural stability.
  • The failure contributed to a major policy shift towards agricultural productivity, food security and the Green Revolution.
📌 Must-Memorise

Third Plan Lesson → Food Security Essential for Development

11. Plan Holiday — 1966–1969

  • The difficulties of the Third Plan led to the Plan Holiday from 1966 to 1969.
  • Three Annual Plans were implemented.
  • Agriculture again received high priority.
  • Food security became a central policy concern.
  • The period coincided with the expansion of the Green Revolution.
📌 Must-Memorise

Plan Holiday → 1966–1969 → Three Annual Plans

12. Green Revolution — Agricultural Turnaround

The Green Revolution expanded through:

  • High-yielding varieties.
  • Irrigation.
  • Fertilisers.
  • Agricultural credit.
  • Modern farming practices.
  • It represented a shift from simple area expansion towards productivity-oriented agriculture.
  • Wheat benefited especially during the early phase.
📌 Must-Memorise

Third Plan Failure → Agricultural Turnaround → Green Revolution

13. Fourth Five-Year Plan — 1969–1974

  • The Fourth Plan aimed at growth with stability and progressive achievement of self-reliance.
  • Major bank nationalisation in 1969 expanded the State's role in financial intermediation.
  • Institutional banking was extended towards previously underserved areas.
  • However, significant inflationary pressures weakened the stability objective.
  • The 1971 war increased public expenditure.
  • The global oil-price shock of the early 1970s raised the cost of imported petroleum.
  • These domestic and external disturbances restricted Plan performance.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fourth Plan → Growth with Stability + Self-Reliance

14. Fourth Plan — Overall Assessment

  • The Fourth Plan tried to combine growth, economic stability and self-reliance.
  • Its outcomes were weakened by inflation, war-related pressures and the international oil shock.
  • Growth objectives were not fully achieved.

15. Fifth Five-Year Plan — Poverty and Basic Needs

  • The Fifth Plan began in 1974.
  • Poverty reduction and self-reliance were central objectives.
  • Garibi Hatao reflected the stronger emphasis on poverty removal.
  • Planning shifted further from a purely growth-oriented approach towards redistribution and basic needs.
  • Minimum Needs Programme sought to improve education, drinking water, health, roads and rural electrification.
  • Twenty-Point Programme focused on poverty reduction and social development.
  • The Fifth Plan was terminated before completion following a change in Government.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fifth Plan → Poverty Reduction + Basic Needs

16. Fourth and Fifth Plans — Broad Assessment

  • These Plans marked an important shift towards poverty reduction, redistribution and minimum needs.
  • Political change, inflation and external disturbances reduced the effectiveness of implementation.

17. Sixth Five-Year Plan — 1980–1985

  • The Sixth Plan focused on poverty reduction, employment, technology, energy and infrastructure.
  • Economic growth strengthened compared with several earlier Plan periods.
  • Productivity and technological development received greater attention.
  • Poverty-alleviation programmes expanded.
  • Rural employment schemes gained greater importance.
  • Employment became a more explicit development objective.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sixth Plan → Stronger Growth + Poverty Reduction + Technology

18. Sixth Plan — Overall Assessment

  • The Plan achieved stronger economic growth and a greater focus on productivity and modernisation.
  • Poverty nevertheless remained widespread.
  • Unemployment continued to be a major structural problem.

19. Seventh Five-Year Plan — 1985–1990

  • The Seventh Plan emphasised Food, Work and Productivity.
  • Telecommunications, computers and modern technologies gained increasing importance.
  • Industrial efficiency and productivity received greater attention.
  • Economic growth strengthened.
  • The private sector gradually acquired a greater role.

20. Seventh Plan — Fiscal and External Weaknesses

  • Government expenditure rose significantly.
  • Government borrowing increased.
  • Fiscal imbalances became more serious towards the end of the 1980s.
  • External borrowing also increased.
  • Balance-of-payments pressures intensified.
  • These accumulated fiscal and external weaknesses contributed to the macroeconomic crisis that emerged in 1991.
📌 Must-Memorise

Late-1980s Imbalances → Contributed to 1991 Crisis

21. Seventh Plan — Overall Assessment

  • The Seventh Plan achieved stronger growth and modernisation.
  • However, rising fiscal and external imbalances weakened macroeconomic stability.

22. Eighth Five-Year Plan — 1992–1997

  • The Eighth Plan was the first regular Five-Year Plan after the 1991 economic reforms.
  • Industrial licensing was reduced in many sectors.
  • Private-sector participation increased substantially.
  • Foreign investment gained importance.
  • Trade and financial-sector reforms increased India's integration with the world economy.
  • Human development, employment, education and health received greater attention.
📌 Must-Memorise

Eighth Plan → Post-Reform Growth + Human Development

23. Eighth Plan — Growth and Structural Change

  • Economic growth during the Plan period was relatively strong.
  • Services expanded significantly.
  • Information technology gained increasing importance.
  • Telecommunications and financial services developed rapidly.
  • Private investment became a stronger source of production and capital formation.

24. Eighth Plan — Continuing Concerns

  • Growth benefits were not distributed evenly across all groups and regions.
  • Employment growth did not always keep pace with output growth.
  • Regional disparities remained significant.
  • Rural-development challenges continued.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Higher GDP Growth ≠ Proportionate Employment Growth

25. Eighth Plan — Overall Assessment

  • The Eighth Plan marked the transition from a more State-directed development framework towards market-oriented and indicative planning.
📌 Must-Memorise

Eighth Plan → Transition to Market-Oriented Indicative Planning

26. Ninth Five-Year Plan — 1997–2002

  • The Ninth Plan emphasised growth with social justice and equity.
  • Agriculture and rural development received significant attention.
  • Poverty reduction and employment remained important objectives.
  • Economic growth was weaker than originally expected.
  • Fiscal problems continued.
  • Infrastructure constraints affected growth.
  • Agricultural performance remained uneven.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ninth Plan → Equity + Rural Development, but Weaker Growth

27. Ninth Plan — Major Lesson

  • The Ninth Plan reinforced the view that growth alone could not eliminate social, rural and regional inequalities.

28. Tenth Five-Year Plan — 2002–2007

  • The Tenth Plan adopted a more explicit system of monitorable development targets.
  • Targets covered poverty, employment, education, health, gender gaps and environmental conditions.
  • Economic growth accelerated during much of the period.
  • Investment increased.
  • Telecommunications and services expanded rapidly.
  • Infrastructure received increased attention.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tenth Plan → Monitorable Development Targets

29. Tenth Plan — Continuing Weaknesses

  • Agricultural growth remained uneven.
  • Employment quality remained a concern.
  • Regional disparities continued despite faster overall economic growth.

30. Tenth Plan — Overall Assessment

  • The Tenth Plan combined faster growth with measurable development outcomes and greater emphasis on governance and implementation.

31. Eleventh Five-Year Plan — 2007–2012

  • The Eleventh Plan adopted Faster and More Inclusive Growth as its central theme.
  • It recognised that high growth was insufficient if large sections of society remained excluded.
  • Education, health, agriculture, infrastructure and employment received attention.
  • Women, children, Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and disadvantaged regions were brought more explicitly into the inclusion framework.
  • Social-sector and infrastructure expenditure expanded.
📌 Must-Memorise

Eleventh Plan → Faster and More Inclusive Growth

32. Eleventh Plan — Major Constraints

  • The global financial crisis of 2008 affected international economic conditions.
  • Inflation remained a concern during parts of the Plan.
  • Infrastructure constraints continued.
  • Governance and implementation problems limited development outcomes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Eleventh Plan External Shock → 2008 Global Financial Crisis

33. Twelfth Five-Year Plan — 2012–2017

  • The Twelfth Plan adopted Faster, More Inclusive and Sustainable Growth as its theme.
  • Environmental sustainability and resource efficiency became more explicit components of planning.
  • Infrastructure and skill development received major attention.
  • Manufacturing, agriculture, health, education and energy remained important priorities.
  • Environmental protection became more directly integrated with economic planning.
📌 Must-Memorise

Twelfth Plan → Growth + Inclusion + Sustainability

34. Twelfth Plan — Institutional Transition

  • Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015.
  • The Twelfth Plan became India's final Five-Year Plan.
  • This marked the end of the traditional Five-Year planning framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

2015 → Planning Commission Replaced

Twelfth Plan → Final Five-Year Plan

35. Agriculture — Long-Term Planning Achievements

Planning contributed to:

  • Expansion of irrigation.
  • Greater agricultural production.
  • Spread of modern inputs.
  • Institutional agricultural credit.
  • Agricultural research.
  • Improved food security.

36. Food Self-Sufficiency — Major Achievement

  • India gradually moved away from chronic dependence on imported food.
  • Green Revolution technologies increased agricultural production, particularly wheat in the early phase.
  • Greater domestic food production strengthened national food security.
📌 Must-Memorise

Major Agricultural Achievement → Greater Food Self-Sufficiency

37. Agriculture — Continuing Weaknesses

Major problems included:

  • Uneven regional productivity.
  • Dependence on rainfall in rain-fed areas.
  • Credit constraints for small farmers.
  • Unequal access to modern technology.
  • Small landholdings.
  • Weak market access.
  • Disguised unemployment.
  • Low farm incomes in many regions.

38. Agriculture — Overall Assessment

  • Five-Year planning substantially improved food security and agricultural infrastructure.
  • Productivity, farm income, rural employment and regional imbalance remained major challenges.
📌 Must-Memorise

Agriculture → Food-Security Success + Productivity and Income Challenges

39. Industry — Long-Term Planning Achievements

Planning helped create capacity in:

  • Steel.
  • Engineering.
  • Machine building.
  • Power generation.
  • Mining.
  • Petroleum refining.
  • Heavy electrical equipment.
  • India developed a diversified industrial base compared with the limited capacity existing at Independence.

40. Public Sector — Industrial Contribution

  • Public-sector enterprises played a major role in industries requiring large capital investment.
  • They helped establish basic and strategic industrial capacity.
  • They also supported infrastructure and technological development.

41. Infrastructure — Long-Term Expansion

The planning era contributed to expansion of:

  • Roads.
  • Railways.
  • Ports.
  • Electricity.
  • Telecommunications.
  • Irrigation.
  • Other basic infrastructure.

42. Industrial Planning — Major Limitations

  • Some public-sector enterprises suffered from low efficiency and weak financial performance.
  • Industrial licensing created delays.
  • Excessive regulation weakened competition.
  • Infrastructure shortages continued despite large investment.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Public-Sector Expansion → Achievement

Public-Sector Inefficiency → Limitation

43. Industry — Overall Assessment

  • Planning created much of the heavy-industrial and infrastructure foundation of modern India.
  • Regulatory rigidities and inefficiencies reduced competitiveness in some sectors.
📌 Must-Memorise

Industrial Planning → Strong Foundation + Regulatory Inefficiencies

44. Poverty Reduction — Long-Term Outcome

  • Poverty reduction became increasingly important across successive Plans.
  • Fifth Plan brought poverty removal more explicitly to the centre of planning.
  • Later Plans expanded programmes for rural employment, food security, housing, education, health and social protection.
  • Poverty declined over the long term.
  • The decline was uneven across States and social groups.
📌 Must-Memorise

Planning → Long-Term Poverty Reduction, Not Elimination

45. Employment — Persistent Development Weakness

  • Employment remained one of the most difficult problems throughout the planning period.
  • Rapid population growth increased labour-market pressure.
  • Early heavy-industry strategy was relatively capital-intensive.
  • Disguised unemployment continued in agriculture.
  • Underemployment and informal employment remained widespread.
  • Employment quality remained a major concern.

46. Human Capital and Employment

  • Later Plans increasingly recognised education, health and skills as necessary for productive employment.
  • Human development gradually became a central component of employment policy.

47. Poverty and Employment — Overall Assessment

  • Planning contributed to long-term poverty reduction and expansion of social services.
  • Employment generation, employment quality and unequal access to opportunities remained major limitations.
📌 Must-Memorise

Poverty Declined → Employment Challenge Continued

48. Self-Reliance — Long-Term Achievement

Planning helped build domestic capability in:

  • Steel.
  • Engineering.
  • Energy.
  • Pharmaceuticals.
  • Agricultural research.
  • Industrial equipment.
  • Technology.
  • India became less dependent on imports for several critical productive capabilities.

49. Structural Transformation

  • Agriculture's relative share in national output gradually declined.
  • Industry and especially services became more important.
  • Scientific and technological capabilities expanded in space, atomic energy, pharmaceuticals, engineering, IT and agricultural research.
📌 Must-Memorise

Structural Transformation → Agriculture Share ↓, Industry and Services ↑

50. Self-Reliance — Meaning Changed After 1991

  • Earlier self-reliance emphasised import substitution and domestic production.
  • After 1991, it increasingly meant developing competitive domestic capability within a more open global economy.
  • Complete economic self-sufficiency was neither fully achieved nor necessarily desirable.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Self-Reliance ≠ Complete Self-Sufficiency

51. Regional Balance — Planning Objective

  • Balanced regional development was a repeated planning objective.
  • Economic development nevertheless remained uneven across States and regions.

Differences persisted in:

  • Industrialisation.
  • Irrigation.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Education.
  • Urbanisation.
  • Income.
  • Employment opportunities.

52. Green Revolution and Regional Inequality

  • Green Revolution benefits were initially concentrated more strongly in regions with better irrigation and infrastructure.
  • Rain-fed regions gained less rapidly.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Green Revolution Benefits ≠ Uniform Across India

53. Industrial Concentration and Regional Disparity

  • Industrial investment tended to concentrate in certain States and urban centres.
  • This reinforced regional differences in income, employment, infrastructure and urbanisation.

54. Social and Economic Inequalities

Persistent inequalities included:

  • Income inequality.
  • Wealth inequality.
  • Unequal access to education.
  • Unequal access to health care.
  • Unequal access to land.
  • Unequal access to institutional credit.
  • Unequal employment opportunities.

55. Policies for Regional Balance

Government attempted to reduce disparities through:

  • Special development programmes.
  • Fiscal transfers.
  • Public investment.
  • Regional-development policies.
  • These measures reduced some gaps but did not eliminate regional and social inequality.
📌 Must-Memorise

Regional Development → Progress + Persistent Disparities

56. First to Fifth Plans — Assessment Memory Chain

  • First → Agriculture + irrigation + stability + relatively successful.
  • Second → Heavy-industrial foundation + agriculture/employment weakness.
  • Third → Wars + drought + food crisis + underperformance.
  • Plan Holiday → Agricultural turnaround + Green Revolution.
  • Fourth → Growth with stability but inflation and external shocks.
  • Fifth → Poverty reduction + basic needs + early termination.

57. Sixth to Twelfth Plans — Assessment Memory Chain

  • Sixth → Stronger growth + poverty programmes + technology.
  • Seventh → Growth + modernisation + fiscal stress.
  • Eighth → Post-reform transition + human development.
  • Ninth → Social justice + rural development + weaker growth.
  • Tenth → Faster growth + monitorable targets.
  • Eleventh → Inclusive growth + 2008 crisis.
  • Twelfth → Inclusion + sustainability + final Plan.

58. Major Long-Term Achievements of Five-Year Planning

Important achievements included:

  • Improved food security.
  • Agricultural modernisation.
  • Expansion of irrigation.
  • Heavy-industry development.
  • Infrastructure expansion.
  • Growth of power generation.
  • Scientific and technological capability.
  • Long-term poverty reduction.
  • Expansion of education and health.
  • Greater domestic productive capacity.
  • Structural transformation.

59. Major Long-Term Limitations of Five-Year Planning

Important limitations included:

  • Persistent unemployment.
  • Informal employment.
  • Rural underemployment.
  • Regional disparities.
  • Income and wealth inequality.
  • Agricultural productivity gaps.
  • Infrastructure shortages.
  • Public-sector inefficiencies.
  • Fiscal imbalances.
  • Unequal access to opportunities.

60. Growth vs Development — Assessment Distinction

  • Economic growth measures the increase in output.
  • Development assessment also examines poverty, employment, human development, inclusion, sustainability and regional balance.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Higher Growth ≠ Complete Development Success

61. Overall Assessment of Five-Year Planning

Major successes:

  • Food security.
  • Industrial foundation.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Scientific capability.
  • Poverty reduction.
  • Human-development expansion.

Major weaknesses:

  • Employment generation.
  • Job quality.
  • Regional inequality.
  • Social inequality.
  • Agricultural productivity gaps.
  • Efficiency problems.

62. Ultra-Short Assessment Memory Chain

  • First → Successful Foundation.
  • Second → Heavy Industry.
  • Third → Failure + Food Crisis.
  • Holiday → Green Revolution.
  • Fourth → Inflation + Shocks.
  • Fifth → Poverty.
  • Sixth → Growth + Technology.
  • Seventh → Growth + Fiscal Stress.
  • Eighth → Reform Transition.
  • Ninth → Equity.
  • Tenth → Targets.
  • Eleventh → Inclusion.
  • Twelfth → Sustainability.

63. TNPSC Traps

  • Plan success cannot be measured by growth alone.
  • First Plan was primarily agriculture-oriented.
  • First Plan is generally regarded as relatively successful.
  • Second Plan created India's heavy-industrial base.
  • Heavy-industry strategy was capital-intensive.
  • Second Plan created pressure on foreign exchange.
  • Third Plan faced both wars and severe drought.
  • Third Plan failure contributed to renewed agricultural priority.
  • Plan Holiday lasted from 1966 to 1969.
  • Green Revolution expanded during the Annual Plan period.
  • Fourth Plan faced inflation, war-related expenditure and oil-price shocks.
  • Fifth Plan strengthened the poverty-reduction and basic-needs approach.
  • Sixth Plan achieved stronger growth but poverty and unemployment remained.
  • Seventh Plan saw rising fiscal and external imbalances.
  • Late-1980s imbalances contributed to the 1991 crisis.
  • Eighth Plan was the first regular Plan after the 1991 reforms.
  • Eighth Plan marked a shift towards market-oriented indicative planning.
  • Ninth Plan emphasised social justice and equity.
  • Tenth Plan emphasised monitorable targets.
  • Eleventh Plan emphasised inclusive growth.
  • Eleventh Plan period included the 2008 global financial crisis.
  • Twelfth Plan emphasised sustainability.
  • Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015.
  • Twelfth Plan was India's final Five-Year Plan.
  • Food security was a major long-term planning achievement.
  • Heavy-industry and infrastructure creation were major achievements.
  • Employment generation remained a major weakness.
  • Regional disparities persisted.
  • Green Revolution benefits were regionally uneven.
  • Public-sector growth was important, but efficiency problems emerged.
  • Self-reliance does not mean complete economic isolation.
  • Economic growth alone cannot determine overall Plan success.

64. Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

  • How should Five-Year Plans be assessed? → Through growth plus economic and social development outcomes.
  • Is achievement of growth target alone sufficient? → No.
  • First Plan assessment? → Relatively successful in agriculture, irrigation and stabilisation.
  • First Plan limitation? → Poverty and low productivity continued.
  • Second Plan's major achievement? → Heavy-industrial foundation.
  • Second Plan's major weakness? → Agriculture, employment and foreign-exchange pressures.
  • Why was Second Plan employment creation limited? → Heavy industry was capital-intensive.
  • Third Plan affected by which wars? → China war of 1962 and Pakistan war of 1965.
  • Other Third Plan problems? → Drought and food shortages.
  • Main lesson from Third Plan? → Food security is essential for development.
  • Plan Holiday? → 1966–1969.
  • Major development during Plan Holiday? → Green Revolution.
  • Fourth Plan objective? → Growth with stability and self-reliance.
  • Fourth Plan constraints? → Inflation, war and oil shock.
  • Fifth Plan focus? → Poverty reduction and basic needs.
  • Sixth Plan achievement? → Stronger growth and modernisation.
  • Sixth Plan weakness? → Poverty and unemployment continued.
  • Seventh Plan achievement? → Growth and modernisation.
  • Seventh Plan weakness? → Rising fiscal and external imbalances.
  • These imbalances contributed to? → 1991 macroeconomic crisis.
  • Eighth Plan significance? → First regular Plan after 1991 reforms.
  • Eighth Plan marked what shift? → Market-oriented indicative planning.
  • Ninth Plan emphasis? → Social justice and rural development.
  • Tenth Plan distinctive feature? → Monitorable targets.
  • Eleventh Plan theme? → Faster and More Inclusive Growth.
  • Major Eleventh Plan external shock? → Global financial crisis of 2008.
  • Twelfth Plan theme? → Faster, More Inclusive and Sustainable Growth.
  • Planning Commission replaced in? → 2015.
  • Replaced by? → NITI Aayog.
  • Final Five-Year Plan? → Twelfth Plan.
  • Major agricultural achievement? → Greater food self-sufficiency.
  • Major agricultural weakness? → Uneven productivity and regional disparities.
  • Major industrial achievement? → Heavy-industrial and infrastructure base.
  • Major public-sector limitation? → Efficiency problems in some enterprises.
  • Major poverty outcome? → Long-term reduction, but not elimination.
  • Major employment weakness? → Inadequate job creation and job quality.
  • Structural transformation means? → Agriculture's relative share declines while industry and services rise.
  • Did planning eliminate regional inequality? → No.
  • Post-1991 self-reliance means? → Competitive domestic capability.
  • Core assessment formula? → Growth + Agriculture + Industry + Employment + Poverty + Human Development + Regional Balance.
